Will winter weather and sea conditions in early 2026 still allow sustained crossing attempts at levels sufficient to generate high death totals?
A) Yes. Weather windows are frequent enough that crossings continue at a high pace despite winter seasonality.
B) No. Winter weather meaningfully suppresses departures and successful launches for much of the period.

Will there be one or more mass-casualty shipwrecks in Jan-Mar 2026 large enough to materially boost the cumulative death count?
A) Yes. Given baseline risk and historical precedent, at least one or several large wrecks are likely enough to push totals toward or above 900.
B) No. Mass-casualty events are too irregular to assume, and without several such disasters the count is unlikely to approach 900 by end-March.

Will the IOM Missing Migrants Project record early-2026 Mediterranean deaths quickly enough that at least 900 are on the books before April, rather than only being added later?
A) Yes. Recording lags will not be so large as to prevent a true early-2026 death toll from appearing in IOM data before April.
B) No. Even if many deaths occur by March 31, reporting and verification lags will keep the IOM recorded total below 900 before April.

Will the volume of attempted Mediterranean crossings in Jan–Mar 2026 be high enough that, even without an extreme disaster, the death toll can approach 900 by April?
A) Yes. Strong push factors and continuing smuggling capacity will sustain enough departures that baseline deaths from ordinary incidents alone could put the total near or above 900 by late Q1 2026.
B) No. Winter seasonality, prior deterrence, economic/political changes, or operational disruption will keep attempted crossings low enough that 900 by April would require unusually extreme events.

Will the fatality rate per attempted Mediterranean crossing in Jan-Mar 2026 be unusually high relative to recent years?
A) Yes. Conditions, vessel quality, smuggler practices, enforcement patterns, or rescue gaps will push the death rate per crossing above recent baselines.
B) No. The death rate per crossing will be at or below recent norms, making 900 by before April hard to reach.

Will geopolitical and domestic conditions in key origin/transit countries by early 2026 generate strong migration pressure rather than suppress departures?
A) Yes. Conflict, repression, economic collapse, and transit-country instability will continue or worsen, sustaining strong outward pressure to attempt crossings.
B) No. Policy, enforcement, seasonal effects, or changing conditions in origin/transit countries will reduce migration pressure and suppress dangerous departures.

Will weather and sea conditions in Jan-Mar 2026 produce unusually high lethality events, including major mass-casualty shipwrecks, rather than a relatively mild quarter?
A) No. Jan-Mar 2026 will not feature enough severe weather interaction or major shipwreck clusters to push deaths to the threshold.
B) Yes. One or more severe weather periods and/or mass-casualty incidents are plausible and could account for a large share of deaths needed to exceed 900.

Will the fatality rate per attempted crossing in early 2026 be elevated relative to recent Mediterranean baselines?
A) Yes. Boats, smuggler practices, enforcement displacement, and conditions will make the death rate unusually high.
B) No. Per-crossing lethality will be closer to or below recent norms due to better vessels, more interceptions, or fewer high-risk voyages.

Will conditions affecting lethality in early 2026 (rescue capacity, smugglers' behavior, vessel quality, enforcement displacement, weather exposure) make deaths per attempted crossing unusually high?
A) Yes. SAR/rescue coverage will be inadequate relative to departures, vessel conditions will remain poor, and policy displacement effects will increase mortality per attempt.
B) No. Mortality per attempt will not be unusually high; rescue activity, deterrence, or calmer conditions will prevent deaths from spiking enough.

Will mortality per attempted crossing on the main Mediterranean routes in January–March 2026 remain at or above recent typical levels rather than improve materially?
A) Yes. Route lethality will stay similar to or worse than recent baselines, due to overloaded boats, smuggling practices, and limited rescue gains.
B) No. Mortality rates will improve materially because of better rescue, interdiction, information, equipment, or route selection.

Will IOM Missing Migrants record major Mediterranean death events quickly enough that deaths occurring in Q1 2026 are mostly reflected in the project totals before April 2026?
A) Most large Q1 Mediterranean death incidents will be incorporated into IOM Missing Migrants totals quickly enough that the before-April threshold mostly tracks deaths occurring by then.
B) A meaningful share of deaths from late-Q1 incidents would not yet be recorded by IOM before April, reducing the chance that the official project total reaches 900 in time.

Will NGO or state search-and-rescue capacity in the Central Mediterranean be materially constrained in early 2026?
A) No. SAR capacity remains available enough that distressed boats are more often reached in time.
B) Yes. SAR coverage is degraded by legal, operational, or political constraints, raising mortality among boats in distress.

Will European and North African migration-control measures in the run-up to and during early 2026 reduce departures more than they increase route danger?
A) Migration-control measures will not reduce departures enough to offset the danger they create or the persistence of flows.
B) Migration-control measures will suppress departures enough that total deaths fall despite any displacement toward riskier routes.

Will conflict, persecution, or economic shocks in key origin/transit countries generate an acute surge in migrants attempting Mediterranean crossings before April 2026?
A) Yes. External shocks increase departures from origin/transit regions, raising pressure on Mediterranean routes.
B) No. No major new push shock occurs; migratory pressure is stable or reduced relative to expectations.

Will the central Mediterranean account for a large majority of Mediterranean crossing deaths in January–March 2026?
A) Yes. The central Mediterranean will remain the overwhelmingly dominant lethal route, with departures from North Africa sustaining high fatality counts.
B) No. Deaths will be more distributed across routes or overall lower on the central Mediterranean, preventing extremely rapid accumulation in the main deadly corridor.

Will one or more large mass-casualty shipwrecks occur before April 2026, materially boosting the cumulative total?
A) Yes. A few high-fatality incidents are likely enough in a three-month window to be an important determinant of whether the threshold is crossed.
B) No. Mass-casualty events are too stochastic to rely on, and absent such a disaster the total is unlikely to reach 900 by end-March.

Will the IOM Missing Migrants Project record deaths in early 2026 at a materially different rate from the true underlying deaths because of changes in detection, reporting, or classification?
A) Yes. Recording is at least as complete as usual, or improves, so elevated deaths are captured in IOM data.
B) No. IOM recording is less complete than assumed, or definitional/reporting changes reduce the number recorded even if true deaths are higher.

Will there be at least one mass-casualty Mediterranean shipwreck in Jan–Mar 2026 large enough to contribute substantially toward the 900-death threshold?
A) At least one very large shipwreck will occur in Jan–Mar 2026, making a large jump in the death toll likely.
B) No exceptionally large shipwreck will occur in Jan–Mar 2026; without such an event, the cumulative toll is unlikely to reach 900 so quickly.

Will the IOM Missing Migrants Project detect and record a large enough share of actual Mediterranean deaths in near real time that true deaths near or above 900 would likely appear in the recorded count before April 2026?
A) Yes. IOM recording will capture most major incidents and enough scattered deaths that recorded totals will track actual deaths reasonably well over the quarter.
B) No. IOM recorded counts may significantly lag or miss deaths, especially in poorly witnessed incidents, so even true deaths near 900 might not appear in the database before April 2026.

Will there be at least one mass-casualty Mediterranean shipwreck or disappearance event before April 2026 large enough to substantially move the recorded total toward 900?
A) Yes. A single large wreck/disappearance is likely enough in a three-month window that tail risk materially boosts the probability.
B) No. The odds of a major mass-casualty event before April are limited, so the total will depend mostly on routine attritional deaths.

Will the IOM Missing Migrants Project record Mediterranean deaths with sufficient completeness and speed that deaths occurring by March 31, 2026 are largely reflected before April ends?
A) Yes. IOM recording will capture a large enough share of Q1 deaths quickly enough for the threshold to be reached in the data.
B) No. Recording lags, undercounting, or limited evidence will keep recorded deaths below the threshold even if true deaths are higher.

Will the fatality rate per attempted crossing in early 2026 be elevated relative to recent Mediterranean norms?
A) No. Crossing volume will remain moderate or seasonally suppressed, making 900 before April unlikely unless lethality becomes extreme.
B) No. Even if crossings occur, lethality per crossing will stay near or below recent norms, keeping totals below the threshold.

Will the Central Mediterranean route account for a large share of Mediterranean crossing attempts in Q1 2026?
A) Yes. The Central Mediterranean will dominate crossings, and it is typically the deadliest major Mediterranean route.
B) No. Crossings will be more dispersed across routes, or the less-deadly Eastern/Western routes will take a larger share.

Will the fatality rate per attempted Mediterranean crossing in early 2026 remain near recent dangerous levels rather than falling materially?
A) Yes. Boats will remain overcrowded, unseaworthy, and poorly supported, so the death rate will stay high enough that a large number of crossings translates into many deaths.
B) No. Even if crossings continue, improved rescue coordination, awareness, equipment, or route changes will keep the fatality rate below the level needed to hit 900 so quickly.

Will attempted Mediterranean crossings in January–March 2026 be at least as high as in the same period of recent high-fatality years?
A) Yes. Attempted crossings in Jan–Mar 2026 stay high or rise relative to recent severe years, keeping exposure large.
B) No. Attempted crossings in Jan–Mar 2026 are materially lower than in recent high-fatality years, reducing exposure.

Do historical Mediterranean annual migrant death totals of roughly 2,000–2,500 make a 900-death total by the end of March an unusually early share of the year?

Do March 2026 weather and sea conditions increase the chance of reaching 900 Mediterranean deaths before April?

By the relevant deadline, will the recorded Mediterranean migrant death count reach 900 in 2026 before the end of March, or only by the end of April?

Are seasonal weather conditions, SAR constraints, policy crackdowns, or major incidents likely to add enough fatalities in March 2026 to push the recorded Mediterranean toll to 900?
